subproblems.title: Operator vs Hilbert–Schmidt norm, distance to a subspace, and the projection trace identity
subproblems.statement:
(i) For all m, k and every linear map A : R^m → R^k, ‖A‖ <= |A|, where ‖A‖ is the operator norm and |A| = (Σ_i |A e_i|^2)^{1/2} = hsNorm A is the Hilbert–Schmidt norm (e_i the standard basis).
(ii) For every linear subspace T ⊆ R^m and v ∈ R^m, |p_{T⊥} v| = dist(v, T), where p_{T⊥} is the orthogonal projection onto T⊥.
(iii) For linear subspaces P, T ⊆ R^m with dim P = dim T, trace(p_{T⊥} ∘ p_P) = (1/2)|p_P − p_T|^2, where |·|^2 = hsNormSq.
subproblems.lean_statement: (∀ (m k : ℕ) (A : Rn m →L[ℝ] Rn k), ‖A‖ ≤ hsNorm A) ∧ (∀ (m : ℕ) (T : Submodule ℝ (Rn m)) (v : Rn m), ‖Tᗮ.starProjection v‖ = Metric.infDist v (T : Set (Rn m))) ∧ ∀ (m : ℕ) (P T : Submodule ℝ (Rn m)), Module.finrank ℝ P = Module.finrank ℝ T → LinearMap.trace ℝ (Rn m) (Tᗮ.starProjection.toLinearMap ∘ₗ P.starProjection.toLinearMap) = hsNormSq (P.starProjection - T.starProjection) / 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. The parent proof (Lemma A) uses three linear-algebra facts:
- the projection trace identity of step 3, trace(p_{T⊥} p_x) = n − trace(p_T p_x) = (1/2)|p_x − p_T|^2 for two rank-n orthogonal projections;
- the comparison ||A|| <= |A| of step 5;
- |x'| = |p_{T⊥}(x − z)| = dist(x − z, T), from its Notation paragraph.
They are proved here for arbitrary m and k. The parent uses m = k = n + ℓ, v = x − z, and P the approximate tangent plane at x.

Setting. R^m = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m), with orthonormal basis e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1.
- hsNormSq A = Σ_i ‖A e_i‖^2 and hsNorm A = (hsNormSq A)^{1/2}.
- Every subspace W of R^m is finite-dimensional, hence complete. So the orthogonal projection p_W := W.starProjection exists.
- p_W is self-adjoint and idempotent, with range W and kernel W⊥, and v = p_W v + p_{W⊥} v for every v.

(i) Operator norm <= Hilbert–Schmidt norm.
1. Let A : R^m → R^k be linear and v ∈ R^m with coordinates v_i. Then v = Σ_i v_i e_i and ‖v‖^2 = Σ_i v_i^2.
2. Linearity, the triangle inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz in R^m give
   ‖A v‖ = ‖Σ_i v_i A e_i‖ <= Σ_i |v_i| ‖A e_i‖ <= (Σ_i v_i^2)^{1/2} (Σ_i ‖A e_i‖^2)^{1/2} = hsNorm A · ‖v‖.
3. hsNorm A >= 0 and step 2 holds for every v. The defining bound of the operator norm (ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_le_bound) then gives ‖A‖ <= hsNorm A.

(ii) Distance to a subspace.
4. Let T ⊆ R^m be a subspace and v ∈ R^m. Since v = p_T v + p_{T⊥} v, we have ‖p_{T⊥} v‖ = ‖v − p_T v‖.
5. Let w ∈ T. Then v − w = (v − p_T v) + (p_T v − w), with v − p_T v ∈ T⊥ and p_T v − w ∈ T. By Pythagoras,
   ‖v − w‖^2 = ‖v − p_T v‖^2 + ‖p_T v − w‖^2 >= ‖v − p_T v‖^2,
   with equality at w = p_T v ∈ T. Hence infDist(v, T) = inf_{w ∈ T} ‖v − w‖ = ‖v − p_T v‖ (Submodule.dist_starProjection_eq_infDist).
6. Steps 4 and 5 give ‖p_{T⊥} v‖ = infDist(v, T).

(iii) The trace identity.
7. Let P, T ⊆ R^m be subspaces with dim P = dim T =: k. Write p := p_P and q := p_T.
   An orthogonal projection onto W is a projection onto W along W⊥, so its trace is dim W (LinearMap.IsProj.trace). Equivalently, in an orthonormal basis adapted to W ⊕ W⊥ its matrix is diag(1,…,1,0,…,0). Hence trace p = trace q = k.
8. Step 4, applied to every vector, gives p_{T⊥} = I − q. So trace(p_{T⊥} ∘ p) = trace p − trace(q ∘ p) = k − trace(qp).
9. Let B be linear on R^m. In the orthonormal basis (e_i) the trace is the sum of the diagonal entries ⟨e_i, C e_i⟩. Hence hsNormSq B = Σ_i ‖B e_i‖^2 = Σ_i ⟨e_i, B^*B e_i⟩ = trace(B^*B).
10. B := p − q is self-adjoint, and p^2 = p, q^2 = q. So B^*B = (p − q)^2 = p − pq − qp + q. Since trace(pq) = trace(qp),
   hsNormSq(p − q) = trace p + trace q − 2 trace(qp) = 2k − 2 trace(qp).
11. Steps 8 and 10 give hsNormSq(p_P − p_T)/2 = k − trace(qp) = trace(p_{T⊥} ∘ p_P). In Lean: LinearMap.trace ℝ (Rn m) (Tᗮ.starProjection.toLinearMap ∘ₗ P.starProjection.toLinearMap) = hsNormSq (P.starProjection − T.starProjection) / 2.
12. Parts (i), (ii) and (iii) together are the stated conjunction. ∎
proof_key_steps: p_{T⊥}v = v − p_T v and p_T v is the nearest point of T to v, so ‖p_{T⊥}v‖ = infDist v T
the trace of an orthogonal projection is the dimension of its range, so trace p_P = trace p_T = k
hsNormSq B = trace(B^*B) and (p − q)^2 = p − pq − qp + q give hsNormSq(p − q) = 2k − 2 trace(qp)
trace((I − q)p) = k − trace(qp) = hsNormSq(p − q)/2

subproblems.title: Smooth step profile on ℝ: 1 on (−∞, 1/2], 0 on [1, ∞), values in [0, 1], 3-Lipschitz
subproblems.statement: There is a C^infinity function φ : R → R such that (i) 0 <= φ(t) <= 1 for every t; (ii) φ(t) = 1 for every t <= 1/2; (iii) φ(t) = 0 for every t >= 1; (iv) φ is 3-Lipschitz, i.e. |φ(s) − φ(t)| <= 3|s − t| for all s, t ∈ R.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∃ φ : ℝ → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) φ ∧ (∀ t, 0 ≤ φ t ∧ φ t ≤ 1) ∧ (∀ t, t ≤ 1 / 2 → φ t = 1) ∧ (∀ t, 1 ≤ t → φ t = 0) ∧ LipschitzWith 3 φ
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Step 1 of the parent proof (Lemma A) fixes a profile φ ∈ C^∞(ℝ, [0, 1]) with:
- φ = 1 on (−∞, 1/2];
- φ = 0 on [1, ∞);
- |φ'| <= 3.
So c_φ = 3 and C = max{16 c_φ^2, 4} = 144. In Lean, ContDiff ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) means C^∞, and LipschitzWith 3 φ (with 3 : ℝ≥0) means |φ(s) − φ(t)| <= 3|s − t|.

Let S := Real.smoothTransition. Mathlib (Analysis/SpecialFunctions/SmoothTransition.lean) gives:
- S is C^∞ (Real.smoothTransition.contDiff);
- 0 <= S <= 1 (Real.smoothTransition.nonneg, Real.smoothTransition.le_one);
- S(s) = 0 for s <= 0 (Real.smoothTransition.zero_of_nonpos);
- S(s) = 1 for s >= 1 (Real.smoothTransition.one_of_one_le).

1. The bump g. Define g(t) := S(12(t − 1/2)) · S(12(1 − t)) for t ∈ ℝ.
  (a) g is C^∞. The maps t ↦ 12(t − 1/2) and t ↦ 12(1 − t) are affine; composing with S and multiplying preserves C^∞. In particular g is continuous, hence interval-integrable on every interval.
  (b) 0 <= g(t) <= 1 for every t, as a product of two numbers in [0, 1].
  (c) If t <= 1/2, then 12(t − 1/2) <= 0, so the first factor and g(t) are 0. If t >= 1, then 12(1 − t) <= 0, so the second factor and g(t) are 0.
  (d) If 7/12 <= t <= 11/12, then 12(t − 1/2) >= 1 and 12(1 − t) >= 1. Both factors equal 1, so g(t) = 1.
2. The normalizing constant. Let c := ∫_{1/2}^{1} g(s) ds.
  - By 1(d), ∫_{7/12}^{11/12} g = ∫_{7/12}^{11/12} 1 ds = 1/3.
  - We have 1/2 <= 7/12 <= 11/12 <= 1, g >= 0, and g is integrable. So the integral over the subinterval is at most the integral over [1/2, 1] (intervalIntegral.integral_mono_interval). Hence 1/3 <= c.
  - Therefore c > 0 and c^{-1} <= 3.
3. The profile. Define φ(t) := 1 − c^{-1} ∫_{1/2}^{t} g(s) ds.
  (a) g is continuous. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (Continuous.integral_hasStrictDerivAt), u ↦ ∫_{1/2}^{u} g has derivative g(t) at every t. So φ is differentiable at every t with φ'(t) = −c^{-1} g(t).
  (b) φ is C^∞. By contDiff_infty_iff_deriv it suffices that φ is differentiable (by (a)) and that deriv φ = −c^{-1} g is C^∞ (by 1(a)).
  (c) φ is 3-Lipschitz. For every t, |φ'(t)| = c^{-1} g(t) <= c^{-1} <= 3, by 1(b) and step 2. The mean value inequality (lipschitzWith_of_nnnorm_deriv_le) then gives |φ(s) − φ(t)| <= 3|s − t|.
4. Values of φ.
  (a) Case t <= 1/2. Every s between t and 1/2 has g(s) = 0 by 1(c). So ∫_{1/2}^{t} g = 0 and φ(t) = 1.
  (b) Case t >= 1. By additivity over adjacent intervals (intervalIntegral.integral_add_adjacent_intervals), ∫_{1/2}^{t} g = ∫_{1/2}^{1} g + ∫_{1}^{t} g. The second integral is 0, since g = 0 on [1, t] by 1(c). So ∫_{1/2}^{t} g = c and φ(t) = 1 − c^{-1}c = 0.
  (c) Case 1/2 < t < 1.
    - g >= 0 and 1/2 <= t give ∫_{1/2}^{t} g >= 0 (intervalIntegral.integral_nonneg).
    - g >= 0 and [1/2, t] ⊆ [1/2, 1] give ∫_{1/2}^{t} g <= ∫_{1/2}^{1} g = c (intervalIntegral.integral_mono_interval).
    - Multiplying by c^{-1} > 0 gives 0 <= c^{-1} ∫_{1/2}^{t} g <= 1, so 0 <= φ(t) <= 1.
  Every real t falls in one of the three cases. In cases (a) and (b), φ(t) ∈ {1, 0}. Hence 0 <= φ(t) <= 1 for all t.
5. Conclusion. φ satisfies every required property:
  - C^∞, by 3(b);
  - values in [0, 1], by 4;
  - equal to 1 for t <= 1/2, by 4(a);
  - equal to 0 for t >= 1, by 4(b);
  - 3-Lipschitz, by 3(c). ∎
proof_key_steps: With S = Real.smoothTransition, g(t) = S(12(t − 1/2))·S(12(1 − t)) is C^∞, 0 <= g <= 1, g = 0 for t <= 1/2 and for t >= 1, and g = 1 on [7/12, 11/12]
φ(t) = 1 − c^{-1}∫_{1/2}^{t} g has φ' = −c^{-1} g by FTC, so φ is C^∞ (contDiff_infty_iff_deriv)
φ = 1 for t <= 1/2, φ = 0 for t >= 1, and 0 <= φ <= 1 in between since 0 <= ∫_{1/2}^{t} g <= c

subproblems.title: The radial lift x ↦ φ(‖x − ξ‖/ρ) of a C^∞ profile with φ = 1 on (−∞, 1/2] is C^∞
subproblems.statement: Let m ∈ N, ξ ∈ R^m (Euclidean space EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)), ρ > 0, and let φ : R → R be C^infinity with φ(t) = 1 for every t <= 1/2. Then the function ζ : R^m → R, ζ(x) := φ(‖x − ξ‖/ρ), is C^infinity.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (ξ : Rn m) (ρ : ℝ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ), 0 < ρ → ContDiff ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) φ → (∀ t, t ≤ 1 / 2 → φ t = 1) → ContDiff ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) (fun x : Rn m => φ (‖x - ξ‖ / ρ))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Step 1 of the parent proof (Lemma A) says: 'Since φ is constant near 0, ζ is C^∞', where ζ(x) = φ(‖x − ξ‖/ρ). It is proved here for general m, ξ and ρ; the parent applies it with m = n + ℓ, ξ = z, ρ = r. Only the two properties of φ used there are assumed: φ is C^∞, and φ = 1 on (−∞, 1/2]. In Lean, ContDiff ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) means C^∞.

1. By contDiff_iff_contDiffAt, ζ is C^∞ iff it is C^∞ at every point. Fix x ∈ R^m. We treat the cases x = ξ and x ≠ ξ.
2. Case x = ξ.
  - Since ρ/2 > 0, the open ball B°(ξ, ρ/2) is a neighbourhood of ξ (Metric.ball_mem_nhds).
  - For y in this ball, ‖y − ξ‖ < ρ/2. As ρ > 0, this gives ‖y − ξ‖/ρ < 1/2, so ζ(y) = φ(‖y − ξ‖/ρ) = 1 by hypothesis.
  - So ζ agrees with the constant 1 on a neighbourhood of ξ. Constants are C^∞ (contDiffAt_const), and being C^∞ at a point depends only on the germ (ContDiffAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq). Hence ζ is C^∞ at ξ.
3. Case x ≠ ξ.
  - Then x − ξ ≠ 0, and y ↦ y − ξ is C^∞.
  - The Euclidean norm of the inner product space R^m is C^∞ at every nonzero point (contDiffAt_norm), in particular at x − ξ. By the chain rule, y ↦ ‖y − ξ‖ is C^∞ at x.
  - Dividing by the constant ρ preserves this (ContDiffAt.div_const), so y ↦ ‖y − ξ‖/ρ is C^∞ at x.
  - φ is C^∞ on ℝ, so it is C^∞ at ‖x − ξ‖/ρ. By the chain rule (ContDiffAt.comp), ζ is C^∞ at x.
4. Every x falls under step 2 or step 3. So ζ is C^∞ at every point, hence C^∞ on R^m by step 1. ∎
proof_key_steps: Reduce to C^∞ at every point (contDiff_iff_contDiffAt)
At x = ξ: ζ ≡ 1 on the open ball B°(ξ, ρ/2), a neighbourhood of ξ, so ζ is C^∞ at ξ (contDiffAt_const.congr_of_eventuallyEq)
At x ≠ ξ: y ↦ ‖y − ξ‖/ρ is C^∞ at x (contDiffAt_norm at x − ξ ≠ 0, chain rule, div_const); composing with the C^∞ map φ gives C^∞ at x

subproblems.title: The radial lift of a K-Lipschitz profile has ‖Dζ(x)‖ ≤ K/ρ everywhere
subproblems.statement: Let m ∈ N, ξ ∈ R^m (Euclidean space EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)), ρ > 0, K ∈ ℝ≥0, and let φ : R → R be K-Lipschitz, i.e. |φ(s) − φ(t)| <= K|s − t| for all s, t. Put ζ(y) := φ(‖y − ξ‖/ρ). Then for every x ∈ R^m the Fréchet derivative of ζ at x satisfies ‖Dζ(x)‖ <= K/ρ (operator norm). In Lean this is fderiv ℝ ζ x, which is 0 wherever ζ is not differentiable.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (ξ : Rn m) (ρ : ℝ) (K : ℝ≥0) (φ : ℝ → ℝ), 0 < ρ → LipschitzWith K φ → ∀ x : Rn m, ‖fderiv ℝ (fun y : Rn m => φ (‖y - ξ‖ / ρ)) x‖ ≤ (K : ℝ) / ρ
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Step 1 of the parent proof (Lemma A) says |∇ζ| <= c_φ/r for ζ(x) = φ(‖x − z‖/r). Here c_φ is replaced by an arbitrary Lipschitz constant K ∈ ℝ≥0 of φ; the parent applies the result with m = n + ℓ, ξ = z, ρ = r and K = 3. Put ζ(y) := φ(‖y − ξ‖/ρ).

1. Lipschitz estimate. Let y, w ∈ R^m.
  - φ is K-Lipschitz and ρ > 0, so
    |ζ(y) − ζ(w)| <= K·|‖y − ξ‖/ρ − ‖w − ξ‖/ρ| = (K/ρ)·|‖y − ξ‖ − ‖w − ξ‖|.
  - The reverse triangle inequality (abs_norm_sub_norm_le) gives |‖y − ξ‖ − ‖w − ξ‖| <= ‖(y − ξ) − (w − ξ)‖ = ‖y − w‖.
  - Hence |ζ(y) − ζ(w)| <= (K/ρ)·dist(y, w).
2. So ζ is Lipschitz on R^m with the nonnegative constant K/ρ.
  - In Lean this is LipschitzWith (K / ρ.toNNReal) ζ, via LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul and step 1.
  - The real value of K / ρ.toNNReal is (K : ℝ)/ρ, by NNReal.coe_div and Real.coe_toNNReal (ρ >= 0).
3. A C-Lipschitz function on a normed space has Fréchet derivative of operator norm at most C at every point (norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz). Where the function is not differentiable, fderiv is 0 and the bound is trivial. With C = K/ρ from step 2, ‖fderiv ℝ ζ x‖ <= K/ρ for every x ∈ R^m. ∎
proof_key_steps: |ζ(y) − ζ(w)| <= (K/ρ)|‖y − ξ‖ − ‖w − ξ‖| <= (K/ρ)‖y − w‖ (φ K-Lipschitz, ρ > 0, reverse triangle inequality)
ζ is LipschitzWith (K / ρ.toNNReal), whose real value is K/ρ
norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz gives ‖fderiv ℝ ζ x‖ <= K/ρ at every x
